French student protesters say government offered them deal, but they want more

Reuters

26 October, 2026 11:30 pm IST

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

By Makini Brice and Inti Landauro PARIS, Oct 26 (Reuters) – French student leaders said the government had offered a package of education proposals on Monday in response to weeks of street protests, but vowed to keep demonstrating as the measures had fallen short of their demands.

Emerging from a meeting with government officials, the students said the proposals included capping the size of some classes, loans for renovating schools and the replacement of a university admissions system they saw as unfair.

“Not all our demands were met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes,” Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, said.

Show Full Article

There was no immediate confirmation of the education proposals from the government. A press conference to announce the details was delayed.

There were no immediate details on how much funding any such education package would require. The hands of President Emmanuel Macron’s minority government are tied by national debt approaching 120% of GDP and high new borrowing needs already making it difficult to agree a budget for next year.

The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of easing after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.

The movement has since expanded, drawing in trade unions and “yellow vest” activists, known for their high-visibility jackets and mass demonstrations against economic pressures including high fuel costs.

Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for November 5.

On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after Saturday’s protests, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centres.

The unrest and the sense among many French that authorities are struggling to keep the peace have further boosted the poll ratings of far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, already the frontrunner in next year’s presidential election.

An opinion poll published Sunday put her on 32%-33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.

FAR-RIGHT GANGS CONFRONT FAR-LEFT ACTIVISTS

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez earlier said 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Saturday and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.

“We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses,” he said. “In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement.”

A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after the country’s sovereign debt was spared a ratings downgrade on Friday by rating agency Moody’s.

But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage despite a calmer weekend.

Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding that sales had fallen by about 80%.

“We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce,” he told Radio Classique.

(Reporting by Sudip Kar-Gupta, Makini Brice and Inti Landauro; Writing by Mark John; Editing by Toby Chopra and Andrew Heavens)

Serbia’s student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?

Reuters

26 October, 2026 10:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Edward McAllister and Aleksandar Vasovic BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) – By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday’s election, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing – something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.

But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?

Show Full Article

The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.

The students’ victory “is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging,” Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.

WINNERS, BUT CAN THEY STICK TOGETHER?

The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024 and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.

Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support, before choosing 250  academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.

The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.

It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia’s former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia’s accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.

Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.

“(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia’s culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.

“We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system.”

REFORMING PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS

Under Serbia’s constitution, the students’ candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.

Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.

State institutions require “detoxification” after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.

Prelevic warned that Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.

Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.

INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS

In Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.

“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector,” Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.

Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia’s four-year-long invasion.

European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.

“I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing – someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.

(Writing by Edward McAllister; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)

Slovakia to develop Russia ties in areas not hit by sanctions, minister says after Moscow talks

Reuters

26 October, 2026 09:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Oct 26 (Reuters) – Slovakia will continue to pursue its national interests and develop cooperation with Russia in areas not affected by sanctions, Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar said on Monday after talks in Moscow with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

Blanar was in Moscow as Slovakia aimed to discuss Russian energy supplies while resuming a cooperation process suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

• The restart of consultations follows repeated trips to Moscow by Prime Minister Robert Fico, whose views stand out in the 27-member EU since the defeat of pro-Russian Hungarian leader Viktor Orban in an April election

Show Full Article

• Energy was a main topic of the renewed intergovernmental commission that held talks on Monday, the Slovak Foreign Ministry said, adding that Blanar was informed that Russia remained ready to fulfil agreed contracts

• Slovakia buys Russian oil and gas but is meant to stop the gas purchases by late 2027 under an EU plan to deprive Russia of financial resources that fund its war in Ukraine

• “The Russian Federation is difficult to replace for the stability of energy supplies not only for Slovakia, but also for global energy trade, which is evident now amid the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz,” Blanar said

• “Slovakia is a member of the European Union and NATO and we respect the rules that bind us, but within those we seek opportunities for cooperation in the interest of Slovakia’s national interests,” he added

(Reporting by Jason Hovet in Prague; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)
